course: Physics (also the forces unit of Physical Science)
subject: science
objective: Use Newton's laws to explain and predict motion: explain why an object moves at constant velocity when the net force on it is zero; analyze cart data to support the claim that a = F_net / m; identify third-law force pairs and explain why they don't cancel; draw a free-body diagram for an everyday situation and decide the direction of the net force from the motion; and calculate acceleration, net force, mass, weight, or a scale reading in an accelerating elevator.
prerequisites: Acceleration as change in velocity per unit time
candidateStandards: Oklahoma Academic Standards for Science, Physics, Motion and Stability: Forces and Interactions, performance expectation 1 (analyze and interpret data to support the claim that Newton's second law of motion describes the relationship among net force, mass, and acceleration). Okla. Admin. Code 210:15-3-82(2)(A), amended effective 2021-09-11 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/oklahoma/OAC-210-15-3-82). Not confirmed: the teacher must verify the current code and its identifier before it is listed under standards.
sources: OpenStax, Physics (high school edition, 2020), Chapter 4, Sections 4.1 Force, 4.2 Newton's First Law of Motion: Inertia, 4.3 Newton's Second Law of Motion, 4.4 Newton's Third Law of Motion, and Ch. 4 Key Equations (https://openstax.org/books/physics/pages/4-key-equations)

OpenStax, College Physics 2e, Section 4.2 Newton's First Law of Motion: Inertia, for the statement of the first law (https://openstax.org/books/college-physics-2e/pages/4-2-newtons-first-law-of-motion-inertia)
misconceptions: A moving object needs a force to keep it moving (motion 'runs out')
Constant velocity requires a net force in the direction of motion
The net force always points in the direction of motion (e.g. a ball thrown upward)
A thrown or hit object carries a 'force of the throw' after it leaves the hand
The heavier object, or the one doing the pushing, exerts the bigger force in an interaction
Third-law pairs cancel, so nothing should be able to move
The normal force on a book and its weight are a third-law pair
A bathroom scale always measures your weight; it reads more whenever the elevator moves up
Mass and weight are the same quantity
modelLimitations: Objects are rigid bodies treated as points for the forces; rotation is ignored.

Friction is a single constant value that opposes sliding; the lesson uses the same limit for starting and sliding friction (real static friction is usually larger). Friction values for wood, carpet, and ice are illustrative, not measured.
The 'No friction' floor and the smooth track are idealizations.
Air resistance is ignored except in the skydiver scenario.
Cart-lab accelerations include a simulated ±4% sensor error so students analyze data rather than read off exact values.
The pull in the cart lab is a constant force (as from a force sensor held by a moving hand), not a hanging mass, so tension equals the stated force.
The skaters' push is a constant force for 0.5 s on frictionless ice.

Elevator accelerations of 2 and 3 m/s² are larger than ordinary passenger elevators use, to make the effect easy to see. The drop-tower ride is a thought experiment with 1.5 s of free fall and constant braking, not a model of any real ride.
g = 9.8 m/s² throughout (Moon g = 1.6 m/s² in one practice problem).
